chapter: Childhood, family and the sounds of New Orleans
title: How the steam calliope works and how Fate Marable played it
summary: Danny describes the steam calliope's copper pipes and how Marable, in a raincoat, made its chords sound full.

story.theme_name: Dance halls, lake camps and riverboat bandstands
story.community_name: Working the Streckfus riverboats with Fate Marable

blocks.x: Well, that's what you heard in the evening. Now, other than that, you heard...
What did the thing look like?
It's a piano with a copper fingerboard, and it's steam, it has steam pipes. It's the same as an organ in church, them big pipes you see with the organ in the

church. But it's run by steam, and the pipes are copper, and the whole mechanism is copper, because it turns green and it's steam. And Fate used to play it with a raincoat on because the steam is poppin' all around you.
He put on his raincoat and his rain-hat and he'd go and sit up under this canopy, and play this calliope on the riverboat.

He was a master. A calliope, there's something about it that the chords seem unfinished, because it's generally two notes of a triad, and you're hittin' at it, you know. You hear it in the circus. But Fate Marable could somehow play it full, so you... He could mix them chords. Nobody's supposed to play a calliope like Fate. He let the tones run into one another, to cover up what was what -- which was a scientific phenomenon to do that, to know how to make those chords, which modern people are doing today, making them hit on organ, to cover up its misgivings. So you heard that.
